lead: A sine source switched on at t = 0 gives two currents at once: a steady sine set by the phasor answer, and a decaying exponential left over from the switching instant. The exponential is not optional. Its starting size K depends on where the sine was when the switch closed. This explains why a transformer or motor can draw a large first peak even though its steady current is modest. The same calculation covers relay coils, capacitor charging through a resistor, and any AC load energised by a switch.
prereq: You need: phasors and impedance from sinusoidal steady state, source-free circuits for the time constant τ, and first-order step response for natural plus forced response.

sections.h3: The complete response is a sine plus an exponential

blocks.text: Write the source as v<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ). V<sub>m</sub> is peak volts, ω is angular frequency in rad/s, t is seconds, φ is the phase at switching in radians. For a series RL circuit, the phasor impedance is Z = R + jωL. Its magnitude is |Z| = √(R² + (ωL)²), and its angle is θ = tan⁻¹(ωL/R). The steady-state current phasor is I = (V<sub>m</sub>∠φ)/Z. In time form, i<sub>ss</sub>(t) = I<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ − θ), where I<sub>m</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/|Z|.

Inductor current cannot jump. The total current is i(t) = i<sub>ss</sub>(t) + K e<sup>−t/τ</sup>, with τ = L/R in seconds. K is an ampere constant fixed by the initial current. At t = 0⁺, i(0⁺) = I<sub>m</sub> sin(φ − θ) + K, so K = i(0⁺) − I<sub>m</sub> sin(φ − θ). This is the whole method.

Series RC works the same way. Now Z = R − j/(ωC), θ = tan⁻¹(1/(ωRC)), and i<sub>ss</sub>(t) = I<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ + θ), because current leads voltage. The time constant is τ = RC. In RC the capacitor voltage cannot jump: v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺) = v<sub>C</sub>(0⁻). Get the initial current from KVL at t = 0⁺, i(0⁺) = (v<sub>s</sub>(0⁺) − v<sub>C</sub>(0⁺))/R, and then put it in K = i(0⁺) − I<sub>m</sub> sin(φ + θ).
i(t) = Im sin(ωt + φ − θ) + K e−t/τ, K = i(0⁺) − Im sin(φ − θ)
I<sub>m</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/|Z| is peak steady current in A; θ is the impedance angle; τ = L/R is the time constant in s; K is the initial offset in A. For RC replace −θ by +θ and τ by RC.

sections.h3: Where the offset comes from: the switching instant

blocks.text: At the switch, the sine part has some value. If that value is not equal to the actual initial current, the difference must be supplied by K e<sup>−t/τ</sup>. So the size of K depends on φ, the source phase at switching. Some syllabi call this transient response under AC excitation.

The largest offset occurs when i<sub>ss</sub>(0) is at a peak, ±I<sub>m</sub>. For a mainly resistive RL circuit this is close to switching at the source peak. For a purely inductive circuit it is switching at the source zero crossing, because current lags by 90°. The gentlest case is i<sub>ss</sub>(0) = 0, which gives K = 0 and no transient. Keep the general rule: compare i<sub>ss</sub>(0) with i(0⁺), not the source value.
After 5τ the exponential is below 1 % of K and is treated as gone; in the example below τ = 0.25 s, so the transient is over in about 1.25 s.

An RLC circuit under AC behaves in the same pattern: the steady state is still a phasor, and the transient is a second-order solution from second-order RLC circuits. It may ring instead of decaying as one exponential.

In the figure, at t = 0 the steady sine is 2 sin(−0.644) = −1.2 A. The exponential starts at +1.2 A. They cancel, so total i(0) = 0 A. The exponential dies in about 5τ = 1.25 s. After that the total current is the phasor answer.
Use this as a check on every solution. At t = 0⁺ the sum must equal the initial current. At t → ∞ the exponential must vanish. If either check fails, K or θ has a sign error.

Switching at the worst instant can nearly double the first peak, but only when τ is long compared with the period, so that K e<sup>−t/τ</sup> has hardly decayed when the sine reaches its first peak. In the worked example it has: the first steady peak comes at t = 0.74 s, where 1.2e<sup>−4 × 0.74</sup> = 0.06 A, so the first peak is only about 2.06 A. The total still starts at i(0⁺) = 0 A. Fuses react to the first peak, so the switching instant matters in real equipment.

figure.caption: The worked example: the steady current 2 sin(3t − 36.9°) A starts at −1.2 A, so an offset 1.2e⁻⁴ᵗ A is needed to make the total start at 0 A. After about 5τ = 1.25 s the offset is gone and only the phasor answer is left.

spec.aria: Plot from 0 to 4 seconds of the steady sine 2 sin of 3t minus 36.9 degrees, the decaying offset 1.2 e to the minus 4t, and their sum, which starts at 0 amperes and joins the sine after about 1.25 seconds.

examples.question: A series circuit has R = 4 Ω and L = 1 H. The source is v<sub>s</sub> = 10 sin 3t V. The inductor current is zero at the switching instant. Find i(t) for t ≥ 0.
steps: Phasor impedance: Z = R + jωL = 4 + j(3)(1) = 4 + j3 Ω.
Magnitude |Z| = √(4² + 3²) = 5 Ω. Angle θ = tan⁻¹(3/4) = 36.9° = 0.644 rad.
Steady current peak I<sub>m</sub> = 10/5 = 2 A. With φ = 0, i<sub>ss</sub>(t) = 2 sin(3t − 36.9°) A.
Time constant τ = L/R = 1/4 = 0.25 s, so the exponent is e<sup>−t/0.25</sup> = e<sup>−4t</sup>.
At t = 0, i<sub>ss</sub>(0) = 2 sin(−36.9°) = −1.2 A. The inductor current is 0, so 0 = −1.2 + K, giving K = 1.2 A.
Total: i(t) = 2 sin(3t − 36.9°) + 1.2 e<sup>−4t</sup> A for t ≥ 0.
examples.answer: i(t) = 2 sin(3t − 36.9°) + 1.2 e<sup>−4t</sup> A for t ≥ 0.
examples.check:
import math
R=4.0; L=1.0; Vm=10.0; w=3.0
Zmag=math.hypot(R,w*L)
theta=math.atan2(w*L,R)
Im=Vm/Zmag
tau=L/R
iss0=Im*math.sin(-theta)
K=-iss0
print(Zmag)
print(round(math.degrees(theta),2))
print(Im)
print(tau)
print(round(iss0,10))
print(round(K,10))

traps: Finding the phasor steady-state current and stopping there. The examiner wants the exponential term and K.
Using K = i(0⁺) − 0 instead of K = i(0⁺) − i<sub>ss</sub>(0). The sine part is not zero at switching in general.
Wrong sign of θ. In RL the steady current lags, so write φ − θ. In RC the current leads, so write φ + θ.
Swapping time constants: τ = L/R for RL and τ = RC for RC. R in ohms, L in henry, C in farad give seconds. In RC, find i(0⁺) from KVL: capacitor voltage cannot jump, but current can.
Assuming the source peak is always the worst switching instant. For a purely inductive circuit the worst instant is the source zero crossing; compare i<sub>ss</sub>(0) with i(0⁺) instead.

quiz.q: State the complete response form for a series RL circuit driven by v<sub>s</sub> = V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ). Define I<sub>m</sub>, θ, τ and K.
quiz.a: i(t) = I<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt + φ − θ) + K e<sup>−t/τ</sup>, where I<sub>m</sub> = V<sub>m</sub>/|Z| is peak steady current, θ = tan⁻¹(ωL/R) is the impedance angle, τ = L/R is the time constant, and K is a constant fixed by i(0⁺).

quiz.q: Why does a decaying exponential appear even though the source is a pure sine?
quiz.a: Switching does not generally match the stored energy to the steady sine value. The difference between the actual initial current and the steady-state sine at t = 0 must be supplied by K e<sup>−t/τ</sup>. That difference decays as the circuit settles.

quiz.q: For a series RC circuit, does the steady-state current lead or lag the source voltage? Why?
quiz.a: It leads. Z = R − j/(ωC) has a negative angle, so the current phase is φ + θ, ahead of the source phase φ.

quiz.q: R = 3 Ω and L = 1 H are in series with v<sub>s</sub> = 5 sin 2t V. The initial current is zero. Find i(t).
R = 2 Ω and C = 0.5 F are in series with v<sub>s</sub> = 10 sin 4t V. The capacitor is initially uncharged. Find K for the current.
A series RL circuit is switched at the instant the source is at a positive peak. Is the transient current always maximum? Explain for R = 0 and for very large R.
quiz.a: No. For R = 0 the current lags the source by 90°, so at the source peak the steady current is zero and K = 0. For very large R the current is almost in phase with the source, so the source peak gives i<sub>ss</sub>(0) near its peak and K is large. The worst instant is where i<sub>ss</sub>(0) is at a peak.

quiz.q: Two identical RL circuits are switched at different source phases. One shows no exponential, the other a large one. What differs, and how do you detect it from i(0)?
quiz.a: The source phase φ at switching differs. If i<sub>ss</sub>(0) equals the actual initial current, K = 0 and no exponential appears. A large exponential appears when i<sub>ss</sub>(0) is far from i(0⁺), with the largest offset when i<sub>ss</sub>(0) = ±I<sub>m</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. Point-on-wave switching uses this calculation to close a breaker when the steady-state current is zero, removing the offset. Transformer inrush is the same idea with a nonlinear core: the flux offset can saturate the core and draw a current many times rated. Motor starters and pre-charge resistors limit the first peak. Power-system software such as EMTP and PSCAD simulates these transients for breaker and insulation studies. Search next: point-on-wave switching, transformer inrush current, DC offset in fault current.
